newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF urges Bulgaria to take steps to boost lev.
newsitem.headline: IMF urges Bulgaria to take steps to boost lev.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) urged Bulgaria to adopt special measures to prop up its slumping national currency, the lev, a senior IMF official said on Monday.

"We are talking with the government about how we can restore confidence in this country and in the lev particularly as part of a broader package," Michael Deppler, Deputy Director of the IMF European Department, told reporters after meeting President Zhelyu Zhelev.
Deppler is part of an IMF mission in Sofia to review the country's reform performance and agree policies that would unblock further funding.

The IMF has twice so far postponed a $115 million loan due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.

"The fund is very concerned about Bulgaria. The situation has been very difficult in past year and the problems have been much bigger and deeper than we or the government had thought they would be," said Deppler.
Delayed structural reforms and a stagnant economy have pressured the lev to 246 to the dollar now from around 70 in January.
"The difficult situation calls for special control over the hard currency regime," said Zhelev's economy advisor Kiril Velev.

"We will need to resort to extremely severe restrictions which will bring about a quick restoration of confidence in the lev...similar measures were applied in Estonia, Lithuania and Argentina and have given good results," said Velev.
These three countries introduced currency boards with help from the IMF to boost credibility in their national currencies.
Under a currency board system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves.
But it also deprives the bank of the usual tools of monetary management, such as market interventions and interest rates.
Deppler said policies were still being discussed but that there was a basic need "for some mechanism to stabilise the exchange rate so that people have confidence in holding levs."

"I go to a (foreign exchange) bureau and all I see is people with huge wallets of levs buying dollars. You cannot run a country when people have those kind of instincts, that must be changed," Deppler said.
In a bid to stabilise the lev, Bulgaria's central bank raised the central interest rate to a record-high 300 percent in September. It is currently 180 percent.
The government has delayed drafting the budget frame for next year due to unpredictability of the interest rate.
